abstract: The effectiveness of genomic prediction in forest trees is often constrained by genotype-by-environment (GE) interactions, particularly when predicting performance in environments not represented in the training population. We evaluated the integration of genomic, enviromic (climatic and soil), and metabolomic (targeted monoterpene) information within multi-environment single-step genomic best linear unbiased prediction (ssGBLUP) reaction norm models to improve prediction in unobserved environments. Models incorporated environmental covariates (W) and genotype-specific responses using linear and nonlinear kernels, including Gaussian and Arc-Cosine formulations. The study examined 12 traits measured on 11,124 trees across four lodgepole pine progeny trials, with 1,490 trees genotyped with 25,099 SNPs. Predictive performance was assessed using leave-one-environment-out cross-validation. Additive genetic correlations among environments revealed substantial GE for early-growth traits and drought-related decline, with correlations frequently below 0.65. Inclusion of environmental covariates reduced variance attributed to site effects, indicating that these descriptors captured environmental heterogeneity. Incorporating GE and genotype-by-environmental covariate (GW) interactions improved model performance, increasing explained phenotypic variance by up to 29.58% and reducing residual variance by up to 3.13% relative to baseline models. Across traits, GE explained more phenotypic variation than GW, contributing on average 2.31% and 0.60%, respectively. Predictive ability was high across models (0.688-0.701), with gains of up to 7.85% when nonlinear kernels were combined with metabolomic covariates, particularly for traits exhibiting stronger GE. Monoterpene profiles yielded predictive performance comparable to climate and soil descriptors, highlighting the potential of integrating genomic, enviromic, and metabolomic information to improve prediction across environments and support climate-resilient forest tree breeding and deployment.
